summary: Defines new RADIUS accounting attributes and new values for an existing attribute to support compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: When dial-in connections are sent through private pipes, this adds new fields to the usage report so those pipes are counted too.

subtitle: New RADIUS accounting values and attributes so an ISP can record when tunnels and tunnel links start, stop or are rejected.

tldr.problem: ISPs that tunnel dial-up users to a customer network without the user asking (compulsory tunneling) need usage records for billing and planning, but RADIUS accounting had no way to describe tunnels.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds six new Acct-Status-Type values (9 to 14) that mark tunnel and tunnel link start, stop and reject events. It also adds two attributes: Acct-Tunnel-Connection (68) identifies the tunnel session, and Acct-Tunnel-Packets-Lost (86) counts lost packets.
tldr.outcome: The ISP and the corporation can each keep matching records, so the corporation can audit the ISP's bill. The memo is Informational and updates RFC 2866.

today: RFC 2867 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2866. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 2867 itself.

sections.title: Why Tunnels Need Accounting
sections.content:
Tunneling protocols such as PPTP and L2TP are often used with dial-up access. With voluntary tunneling, the tunnel is created at the user's request. With compulsory tunneling, it is created as a service of the ISP, without any action or choice from the user.

ISPs usually want usage data for billing and network planning. RADIUS Accounting (RFC 2866) lets that data be collected centrally instead of on each NAS. This RFC defines new attributes and new values of the Acct-Status-Type attribute to describe tunnels. It points to RFC 2809 for specific advice and examples for L2TP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tunnels are built because you asked for one, and others are built for you by your internet company. Either way, the company wants to keep a record of how much each tunnel was used.

sections.title: New Acct-Status-Type Values
sections.content:
Six new values mark tunnel events in Accounting-Request packets. All of them MAY be used, and for each the RFC lists attributes that SHOULD also be included, such as User-Name, NAS-IP-Address, Event-Timestamp, Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Client-Endpoint, Tunnel-Server-Endpoint and Acct-Tunnel-Connection.

  • Tunnel-Start (9) marks establishing a tunnel with another node.
  • Tunnel-Stop (10) marks destroying one. It adds usage counters such as Acct-Input-Octets, Acct-Session-Time and Acct-Tunnel-Packets-Lost.
  • Tunnel-Reject (11) marks a rejected tunnel establishment.
  • Tunnel-Link-Start (12), Tunnel-Link-Stop (13) and Tunnel-Link-Reject (14) do the same for a link inside a tunnel.

Only some tunnel types, such as L2TP, carry multiple links per tunnel. If a tunnel carries M links over its lifetime, 2(M+1) accounting messages might be sent: one pair for the tunnel and one pair for each link. For a single-link tunnel, such as IPsec in tunnel mode, the link values need not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The log gets new check-boxes: tunnel opened, tunnel closed, tunnel refused. There are matching ones for each lane inside a tunnel that has many lanes.

sections.title: The Two New Attributes
sections.content:
Acct-Tunnel-Connection (type 68) holds an identifier for the tunnel session. It SHOULD be included in Accounting-Request packets whose Acct-Status-Type is Start, Stop or any of the new values. Its String format depends on the Tunnel-Type. For L2TP, the Tunnel ID and Call ID might be encoded there, and the exact encoding is implementation dependent.

Acct-Tunnel-Packets-Lost (type 86, length 6) carries a 4-octet count of packets lost on a link. It SHOULD be included when Acct-Status-Type is Tunnel-Link-Stop.

The RFC's attribute table says that tunnel attributes appear in Accounting-Request packets, zero or one time each, and that no tunnel attributes should be found in Accounting-Response packets.
sections.plainLanguage: One new box holds a name tag for the tunnel trip. The other holds a number saying how many packages got lost along the way.

sections.title: Auditing and Call-Serial-Number
sections.content:
A corporation may contract an ISP to provide remote intranet access through compulsory tunneling. If both sides send RADIUS accounting, each gets a record of the user's resource consumption, and the corporation can audit the ISP's bills. The attributes User-Name, Acct-Tunnel-Connection, Tunnel-Client-Endpoint and Tunnel-Server-Endpoint typically identify the call, so the NAS's Accounting-Request can be matched with the tunnel server's.

For L2TP and PPTP, the Call-Serial-Number SHOULD be used in Acct-Tunnel-Connection. In L2TP it is a 32-bit field and in PPTP a 16-bit field. A 16-bit value can wrap: with a NAS of 96 ports that are always busy and an average call of 20 minutes, the RFC works out that it wraps in 9.48 days. So a 16-bit number cannot tell one call from all others over a long period.
sections.plainLanguage: Both the delivery company and the customer keep a log. Matching the two logs by trip number lets the customer check the bill, but small trip numbers run out and start over after a while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC gives a single concern. By sniffing RADIUS Accounting packets, an eavesdropper might perform a passive analysis of tunnel connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who peeks at the trip log could learn who is using tunnels and when.

items.label: Tunnel-Start
items.desc: A tunnel with another node is established.

items.label: Tunnel-Stop
items.desc: A tunnel to or from another node is destroyed.

items.label: Tunnel-Link-Start
items.desc: A link in a tunnel is created.

items.label: Tunnel-Link-Stop
items.desc: A link in a tunnel is destroyed.

items.label: Tunnel-Link-Reject
items.desc: A new link in an existing tunnel was rejected.
